worlds.general: Ottilie Varnhagen and her partner Jorrit Aldemere own a townhouse at 14 Fennimore Row, Halden Cross, and rent the upstairs room to a lodger, Perry. In early October 2026 they are deciding whether to accept a kitchen renovation quote from Halvering & Stroud Kitchens (estimator Dunmore Kessane; Revision C of 22 September 2026 replaced a June Revision A), planning a long weekend at Marrowby Point from 22 to 25 October, having Jorrit's car's front brakes done at Tallowick Auto Service, and keeping an October household budget with a kitchen fund, a trip fund and an approved home improvement loan. Their homeowners association issued renovation rules in September 2026. The user of Natively is Ottilie, an ordinary person with no specialised role.
worlds.sales: Kestravane, Inc. is a fictional B2B SaaS company selling Kestravane Fleet, a fleet-operations platform (vehicle tracking, fuel and idle analytics, maintenance planning, cold-chain temperature monitoring) with optional hardware: TrakNode telematics units, TempSense temperature sensors and RoadLens cameras. It is sold per vehicle per month in three plans (Launch, Operations, Enterprise). The user is a Kestravane account executive talking to prospects and customers. The pack holds the current price list (v4.2, 1 July 2026), the superseded 2025 price list (v3.1), an unapproved draft 2027 price list, the current integration matrix, a security and compliance overview, the support and service level guide, the implementation guide and one customer story (Hollowmere Produce Logistics). Dorrowick Telematics and Pennoway Fleet are fictional competitors; nothing about their products or prices is documented.
worlds.recruiting: Kestrelwick Systems, Inc. is a fictional company of about 310 people in Duluth, Minnesota (hub in Chattanooga, Tennessee) that builds Coldline, a routing and temperature-compliance platform for refrigerated freight. It is hiring one role, Engineering Lead, Ingestion Platform (requisition ENG-2026-0417), a people-manager role reporting to Idris Halvorsen-Peake, Director of Data Platform. The user is the recruiter, Pernille Aubrecht, running the recruiter screen in early October 2026. The other party is the candidate, Ottoline Vaskirk, currently Engineering Team Lead at the fictional Halcyard Freight Cloud in Madison, Wisconsin. The pack holds the approved job description, her resume, the interview scorecard, a candidate-shareable team brief, the current Total Rewards overview (version 4.1, 2026), last year's Total Rewards overview (version 3.2, 2025, outdated, distinguishable only by its version and date), the engineering recruiting process guide, and the hiring manager's informal notes, which conflict with the job description on on-call. The scorecard and the process guide, both current, genuinely disagree on the panel decision rule.
worlds.team-meet: Farrowgate Systems is a fictional software company. Its mobile team builds Mossgauge, an inspection app that utility field crews use on Android and iOS to record site visits, photograph defects and file reports. The pack describes release 3.0 in early October 2026: Sprint 41 (28 September to 9 October) is in its second week, the feature freeze is planned for Friday 9 October, release candidate 1 for Wednesday 14 October, a closed beta with three pilot customers from 15 to 28 October, store submission on Thursday 29 October and launch (start of a staged Android rollout) on Tuesday 3 November. THE USER is Ilka Vantongeren, Android lead and release captain for 3.0: she owns the Android workstream (since Monday 7 September 2026, taking over from Petra Hollowbrook), owns risks R-01 and R-07, makes the go/no-go call with the product manager and may halt or resume the rollout, but may not change the rollout stages without Halvard Niemczyk's approval. The other people in the meetings are colleagues: Halvard Niemczyk (engineering manager), Saoirse Lindqvang (product manager, keeps the decision log), Dorrin Ashgrove-Patel (iOS lead, store submission), Tobiah Kessenich (backend and sync), Yevgenia Marchetti-Oduya (report export), Lucinda Farthingale (photo annotation, sync cover), Corbin Thistlewood (QA lead) and Emeka Rautavaara (design). The live meeting in the items is the weekly team sync of Monday 5 October 2026. The decision log is the approved source of record; the Sprint 37 report (14 August 2026) is outdated; the channel export (1 to 8 September 2026) is informal chat that predates the decisions; the rollout gates note is an unapproved draft. Natively is never told who the user is except through the question or the heard conversation, so items that expect a first-person answer address the user by name.
worlds.looking-for-work: Candidate-owned reference files for the two fictional job candidates of the profiles pack. Advik Thorambath (backend, Hyderabad, Quillhaven Freight Systems) is interviewing at Ostrakel Payments for Senior Backend Engineer on Ledger Core; his private prep notes hold what his résumé omits: why he is looking, a relocation limit (only Bengaluru or Hyderabad), notice period (90 days, corrected from an earlier 60), salary expectation in INR lakh, leadership preference, one weakness and four real stories; his research notes cover Ostrakel. Catarina Velmonte (frontend, Porto, Lumenquay) is interviewing at Hollowpine Labs; her notes hold different reasons, a firm no to relocation, a salary ask in EUR (revised upward in a dated addition), a start date pushed back by a release, and four different stories; her research notes cover Hollowpine and Inkwharf. Also in the folder: an older export of Advik's CV dated 18 January 2024 that disagrees with his current résumé on title, team, on-call rota, migration size and GitHub stars, and the rental-agreement summary for his Hyderabad flat, which has nothing to do with interviewing. Deliberately absent from every file and from both résumés and postings: visa or citizenship status, other offers or interviews in progress, Advik's current salary, Catarina's reason for leaving earlier employers, age, marital status and references.
worlds.lecture: Tavish Orrenby is a second-year student at the fictional Tarnhollow University, taking three courses in Autumn term 2026: CNW 2140 Computer Networks (Dr. Oleska Brantigern), ECN 1620 Prices, Markets and Money (Prof. Tobiah Kessandru) and BIO 1380 Cells, Energy and Heredity (Dr. Maelis Underhaye). His Lecture-mode reference files are the lecture 7 slide deck on TCP congestion control, the networks lecturer's running notes on DNS and HTTP with follow-ups from lecture 7, this year's and last year's CNW 2140 syllabus, the economics lecture 5 slides on inflation and monetary policy, the economics professor's notes on elasticity, this year's and last year's ECN 1620 formula sheet, and the biology lecture notes on cellular respiration and Mendelian genetics. Each lecturer uses course-specific conventions (an initial window of 2 segments and a 1,200-byte MSS; queries-only DNS counting; the midpoint method with positive elasticities; a 'classroom rule' with weights 0.5 and 0.25 and a neutral rate of 1%; 30 ATP per glucose; a marsh-beetle cross with R/r notation), their own worked examples, and a few loose statements that the notes later pin down. There is no syllabus for ECN 1620 or BIO 1380 in the pack. Everything is fictional.
worlds.technical-interview: Reference files a candidate keeps for technical interviews. Candidate A, Advik Thorambath (backend, Quillhaven Freight Systems), has his own as-built notes on Skeinrouter, the Go and Kafka tracking pipeline from his résumé, and an early design proposal for it from May 2024 whose planned values (24 partitions keyed by carrier, a 25,000 events per second target, DynamoDB, 3 brokers, exactly-once transactions) were not what was built. Candidate B, Catarina Velmonte (frontend, Lumenquay), has her notes on Fernlatch, the booking-flow rebuild from her CV. Both also hold neutral interview material: a design brief with fixed requirements for a short-link service and a notification system, a sheet of four coding problems, and three code files that each contain one deliberate defect (a tier-pricing logic bug in Python, an N+1 query loop in TypeScript, a check-then-act lost update in Go). One unrelated document, another company's on-call onboarding checklist, is used as a tempting irrelevant file. Everything is fictional.
worlds.seminar: A fictional research project: TERN, a fault detection and isolation method for air-handling units in school buildings that combines a per-unit thermal-balance model with conformal change detection. The presenter is Maelis Thornquist, a researcher at the Halvard Laboratory for Building Analytics, Kestrelmoor Institute of Technology (co-authors Juho Raskinen and Odalys Brennecke). The data are 17 months of trend logs from 86 units in 14 schools of the Brackenfirth Borough Council estate; five whole buildings are held out. The final paper (camera-ready, 11 September 2026, SBSA 2026) reports F1 0.87 and a median detection delay of 34 minutes against a rule set (0.71, 126 minutes), an LSTM autoencoder and PCA; a March 2026 draft abstract and a March results export carry older figures (F1 0.82, 48 minutes). The pack also holds the seminar slides (8 October 2026), the supplementary material, the final results table and informal reading notes about other groups' systems (Corvane-Net and others), none of which was run on the study's data.
worlds.call-center: Brindlewatch is a fictional consumer company (warehouse in the invented town of Tolliver Falls, US) that sells home security cameras - Lantern Cam (indoor), Eave Cam (outdoor, battery) and Trek Cam (portable, cellular) - with Keep subscriptions (Basic, Plus, Pro; monthly or annual) and a cellular add-on, Roam Link, that charges per-camera, per-calendar-day Roam Day fees abroad. The user is a Tier 1 Customer Care agent on live calls. The pack is the agent's policy shelf: verification, refunds, shipping, account recovery, privacy and camera access, escalation, billing and travel rates, an outage and troubleshooting guide, and a 2025 Support Policy Handbook that is outdated on verification and refunds. Two current documents genuinely disagree on how long Identity Review takes (3 vs 5 business days). All names, people and policies are invented.
worlds.profiles: Two unrelated fictional job candidates and the roles they are interviewing for. Candidate A, Advik Thorambath, is a backend and distributed-systems engineer in Hyderabad with six years of experience (Quillhaven Freight Systems since March 2023, Tessarine Mobility before that) who works in Go and Kotlin on PostgreSQL and Kafka; he is interviewing for Senior Backend Engineer, Payments & Ledger, on the Ledger Core team of Ostrakel Payments in Bengaluru. Candidate B, Catarina Velmonte, is a lead frontend and product engineer in Porto with nine years of experience (Lumenquay since June 2022, Ondaverde Health and Plumewright Studio before that) who works in React, TypeScript and Vue with a focus on accessibility, design systems, frontend performance and product experimentation; she is interviewing for Senior Product Engineer, Collaborative AI Workspace, on the Workspace Surface squad of Hollowpine Labs (Rotterdam, remote within Europe). The two candidates share no employer, project, city, university, technology emphasis or metric value. Neither résumé nor job description states the candidate's reason for leaving, relocation preference, notice period, salary expectation, visa status, weaknesses, or any conflict, failure or mentoring story.

files.title: Brindlewatch Billing Guide and Roam Link Rates v2.4

facts.statement: Keep Basic costs $6 per month or $60 per year, covers 1 camera and keeps 14 days of clips.
Keep Plus costs $13 per month or $130 per year, covers up to 5 cameras and keeps 30 days of clips.
Keep Pro costs $22 per month or $220 per year, covers up to 20 cameras and keeps 60 days of clips plus continuous recording.
Without a plan a camera gives live view and alerts but nothing is recorded.
A monthly plan bills on the same day of each month as it started, or the last day of a shorter month.
Moving up on a monthly plan takes effect at once and is charged (new monthly price - old monthly price) x days remaining / 30, every month being treated as 30 days.
Moving down on a monthly plan takes effect on the next billing date with no credit for the current month.

facts.statement: Roam Link costs $5 per camera per month and covers the United States.

Extra Roam Link data is $4 per GB, with a part GB rounded up to a whole one.
doc_needles: rounded up to a whole one

facts.statement: The Zone 1 (Canada, Mexico) Roam Day fee is $10 per camera per day.
The Zone 2 (United Kingdom, Ireland, European Union) Roam Day fee is $15 per camera per day.
Roam Day fees are capped per camera per billing cycle at $60 in Zone 1 and $90 in Zone 2; the cap counts Roam Day fees only.
doc_needles: cap counts Roam Day fees only

facts.statement: A Roam Week pass costs $45 per camera in Zone 1 and $70 per camera in Zone 2 and covers one camera for 7 consecutive calendar days from activation.
A Roam Week pass has to be activated before the camera first connects abroad and cannot be added to a trip afterwards.
doc_needles: before the camera first connects abroad

facts.statement: Days abroad outside the pass's 7 days are charged as Roam Days.
A Roam Day is a calendar day, midnight to midnight in the account's home time zone, not a 24-hour period from first connection.
doc_needles: A day is a calendar day

facts.statement: Any connection to a partner network on a day, however short, makes it a Roam Day.
Each Trek Cam is charged Roam Day fees separately.
doc_needles: Each Trek Cam is charged separately

facts.statement: A camera that is switched off or set to Wi-Fi only is not charged.
Roam Link does not work outside the United States, Zone 1 and Zone 2.
doc_needles: does not work in other countries

facts.statement: Invoice lines read ROAM DAY Z1 or ROAM DAY Z2 and the quantity is camera-days.

First-trip courtesy: if the invoice is the account's first ever with Roam Day fees, a Tier 1 agent may credit up to $30 of them, once per account.
Any larger travel-charge adjustment, or a second request, goes to Billing Operations (Tier 2), and the agent does not say what Billing Operations will decide.

files.title: Customer Care Escalation Matrix v6

facts.statement: Tier 1 verifies callers, handles plan and billing enquiries, plan changes, refunds within its limit, order status, carrier traces and the six troubleshooting steps; most contacts should end at Tier 1.

A device fault goes to Tier 2 Device Diagnostics when all six troubleshooting steps are done and the fault remains, when the light is solid red, or when it is the customer's third contact about the same fault within 14 days even if the steps were not all repeated.
doc_needles: All six troubleshooting steps are done
third contact about the same fault

facts.statement: Tier 2 Account Integrity takes Identity Review (IR-7), power of attorney or guardianship, and accounts of holders who have died.
Tier 2 Billing Operations takes refunds that cannot reach the original payment method, chargebacks, invoice errors and travel-charge disputes beyond the first-trip courtesy.
doc_needles: travel-charge dispute beyond the first-trip courtesy

facts.statement: Tier 2 Order Integrity takes a second delivered-but-missing claim within 12 months and suspected reselling or fraud.
Tier 2 handover is a warm transfer Monday to Saturday, 8:00 am to 8:00 pm Central; outside those hours a ticket, with first contact within 1 business day.
Before handing over the agent writes up what was reported, steps done, and firmware version and light colour for a device fault.
Tier 1 never contacts Engineering; only Tier 2 opens an Engineering case, when a defect is reproduced on 5 or more accounts on the same firmware version or recordings have been lost.
Engineering has no customer-facing response target; agents do not quote a fix date or a firmware release date.
doc_needles: do not quote a fix date

facts.statement: Security cases go straight from Tier 1 to the Trust & Security desk, not through Tier 2; the desk is staffed 24 hours a day, every day, and every case is Priority 1.

Security triggers: someone else in the account or watching cameras, login e-mail changed without the customer, an unfamiliar voice through a camera's speaker, an unrecognised device in the Devices list, danger from someone with access, a reported security weakness.
doc_needles: an unfamiliar voice has come through

facts.statement: The agent warm-transfers and stays on the line until Security answers; if nobody answers within 10 minutes the agent opens a Priority 1 ticket and tells the customer Security will call back within 1 hour.
In security cases the agent does not troubleshoot, reset passwords or remove devices.
If a customer asks for a supervisor the agent never refuses; if none is free a supervisor calls back within 4 business hours.
A refund above the Tier 1 approval limit, or any refund exception, goes to a supervisor.
A Tier 1 agent may give a goodwill credit of up to $25, once per account in any 3 months; more needs a supervisor.
If the customer threatens legal action or the press, the case goes to a supervisor, who informs Legal Response.
A caller who remains abusive after 2 warnings goes to a supervisor.
Deletion and data-copy requests go to the Privacy Office; anything from police, courts or lawyers goes to Legal Response and is never handled on the call.
When escalating, the agent gives the ticket number, the team name and that team's response target, and does not promise an outcome or a resolution time.
The Escalation Matrix is version 6, effective 10 August 2026.
If unsure which Tier 2 desk applies the agent asks in the Tier 2 duty channel before transferring.

must_not_infer: A response target is when a team first responds, not when the problem is resolved.
This document does not state the Tier 1 refund approval limit as an amount.
An upset or angry caller is not an abusive caller.
Nothing here gives customers a fix date or an Engineering contact.

files.title: Brindlewatch Privacy and Camera Access Policy v5.0

facts.statement: No Brindlewatch employee or contractor, at any tier, can watch a customer's live view; no internal tool opens a live stream.
doc_needles: can watch a customer's live view

facts.statement: The live stream is encrypted between the camera and the devices signed in to the customer's account.
Recorded clips are stored encrypted; Tier 1 agents cannot open, play or download a clip and the console shows no video, still images or audio.
doc_needles: no still images and no audio

facts.statement: With Share with Support the customer shares one clip, which can be viewed for 72 hours only by the Tier 2 Device Diagnostics engineer assigned to the ticket; every viewing is logged and the customer can withdraw the share.
Staff can see a recording in only two situations: the customer shares it, or the law requires it.
Agents can see whether a camera is online, when it was last online, firmware version, the plan and the daily count of motion events.
Keep Basic clips are kept for 14 days.
Keep Plus clips are kept for 30 days.
Keep Pro clips are kept for 60 days.
Cancelling a plan does not delete the clips already recorded; each stays until its own retention period runs out.
Customers delete their own recordings in the app under Settings > Privacy > Delete all recordings, after entering the account password.
Deleted clips disappear from the account immediately, are erased from primary storage within 24 hours and from backups within 30 days; deletion cannot be undone.
Agents cannot delete recordings from the support console.

If the customer cannot use the app the Tier 1 agent completes step-up verification and files a Deletion Request (form DR-2); the Privacy Office carries it out within 4 business days and confirms by e-mail.
Erasing an entire account is a separate request to the Privacy Office, completed within 30 calendar days.
Recordings under a legal preservation order are held until it ends; Tier 1 agents are not told which accounts and refer enquiries to the Privacy Office.
Every request from police, a government body, a court or a lawyer is handled only by the Legal Response team at legalresponse@brindlewatch.example.

doc_needles: does not confirm whether the person

facts.statement: Recordings are handed over only in response to a search warrant or court order; a subpoena obtains basic account details only, never video.
Where there is imminent danger of death or serious physical injury, Legal Response alone may disclose without a court order and can be reached around the clock.
The account holder is told before disclosure unless the law forbids it.
A customer who wants the police to have their own footage can download the clips and hand them over themselves.
Sound recording is off by default on Eave Cam.
doc_needles: Sound recording is off by default

facts.statement: Familiar Faces is opt-in and its data can be erased by the customer.
Brindlewatch does not sell customer data or video.

files.title: Password and Account Recovery Procedure v2.3

facts.statement: Agents cannot see, read out or set a customer's password; they can trigger a reset e-mail from the console.
doc_needles: cannot see, read out or set

doc_needles: do not change the e-mail back

facts.statement: Security freezes the account (signs out every session, pauses Shared Access) and restores it to its owner.

A sign-in from a new device sends an alert e-mail; the customer can use Sign out everywhere, and an alert the customer cannot explain goes to the Trust & Security desk.
Shared Access lets the account holder invite up to 4 guests who can watch live view and clips but cannot change settings, delete anything or see billing.
The Password and Account Recovery Procedure is version 2.3, effective 20 April 2026.

The 72-hour block and the 7-day reversal link are not a promise of when Security will restore an account.
Shared Access guests are not Authorised Contacts.

files.title: Brindlewatch Refund and Cancellation Policy v3.1

After the annual refund window there is no refund for the unused part of the term; the plan stays active until the term ends and auto-renew can be switched off.

facts.statement: A camera bought directly can be returned for any reason within 60 days of the delivery date.

files.title: Brindlewatch Account Verification Standard v4.2

facts.statement: Standard verification requires the caller to give 3 of the 5 listed identifiers correctly before anything account-specific is discussed.
The five identifiers are: full name on the account, login e-mail address, billing postal code, last four digits of the payment card on file, and the serial number of a registered camera.

facts.statement: Agents never ask for a password, a full card number, an expiry date or a security code.
After 2 failed attempts in the same contact the agent stops; the account is locked for phone and chat verification for 24 hours and the caller is pointed to Identity Review.
Step-up verification is a 6-digit one-time code sent to the phone number or e-mail address on file; it expires after 10 minutes.

Step-up verification is required before changing the login e-mail, adding or removing an Authorised Contact, filing a recordings Deletion Request, changing the delivery address on an open order, or closing the account.
doc_needles: delivery address on an open order

facts.statement: Only the account holder or a registered Authorised Contact may be helped with an account; spouses, partners, children, parents, housemates, landlords and installers are third parties however much they know and wherever they live.

facts.statement: With a third party the agent gives general product and policy information only, does not confirm that an account exists, and invites them to have the account holder call or to be registered as an Authorised Contact.

facts.statement: An account can have up to 2 Authorised Contacts, added by the account holder in the app or on a verified call after a step-up code.
An Authorised Contact is verified by their own name plus a 4-digit contact PIN.
An Authorised Contact may get troubleshooting help, check order status and billing status, and ask for a carrier trace.

facts.statement: An Authorised Contact may not change the login e-mail or password, receive a reset link, change the payment method, delete recordings, request a refund or close the account.
Power of attorney, guardianship and accounts of customers who have died are handled by Tier 2 Account Integrity on documents; Tier 1 makes no change.

A customer who cannot reach the e-mail on file is verified with 3 of 5 identifiers and then sent the step-up code by text message to the phone number on file; after that the login e-mail can be changed.
With no phone number on file the route is Identity Review (form IR-7): government photo ID plus proof of purchase or a photo of a camera's serial label, decided by Tier 2 Account Integrity.
The Verification Standard tells agents to say Identity Review takes up to 5 business days.
A Tier 1 agent never changes a login e-mail without a confirmed step-up code or an approved IR-7.
A call through a telephone relay service or video relay interpreter is treated as the customer speaking; the relay operator is not asked to verify.

On an assisted call a helper may speak for the account holder provided the account holder is present and consents, by voice or by replying YES to the consent message sent to the phone or e-mail on file.
The helper may relay the account holder's identifiers, and the consent covers that call only.
Any customer may continue by live chat or by e-mail to the address on file, which agents offer unprompted when hearing is the difficulty; one-time codes can go by text message.
Reset links, one-time codes and security notices are sent only to the contact details on file, including during an assisted call, and never to a helper's e-mail address or phone.

A business account is verified through its named administrator; other employees are third parties.
Ticket notes record which identifiers were used, never their values.

files.title: Fennimore Row Homeowners Association — interior renovation rules and 2027 assessments

facts.statement: The notice is dated 1 September 2026, adopted by the Board on 25 August 2026, and applies to work beginning on or after 1 October 2026.

Work that changes a structural or party wall, a shared plumbing stack, the roofline, a window or exterior door opening, or anything visible from outside needs written approval from the Architectural Committee, which answers within 30 days.
Interior work that touches none of those, including replacing a kitchen where fixtures stay on their existing supply and drain locations, does not need Committee approval.
Such interior work needs a Renovation Notification Form filed with the management office at least 14 days before work begins.

The form must be accompanied by the contractor's name, license number and dates, and a certificate of liability insurance showing at least $1,000,000 in general liability cover naming the Association as certificate holder.
Permitted working hours on weekdays are 8:30 am to 5:00 pm.
Saturday work is allowed from 10:00 am to 2:00 pm, quiet work only, with no demolition and no power saws.

files.title: BIO 1380 lecture notes, lectures 8 and 9 (cellular respiration; Mendelian genetics)

facts.statement: Dr. Maelis Underhaye's notes for BIO 1380 lectures 8 and 9 were posted on Friday 2 October 2026.
Lecture 8, on cellular respiration, was on Thursday 24 September 2026.
The four stages and their places: glycolysis in the cytosol; pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The lecturer says 'citric acid cycle'; the course text calls it the Krebs cycle.
Glycolysis yields 2 ATP net (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH per glucose.
Pyruvate oxidation yields 2 NADH and 2 carbon dioxide per glucose.
The citric acid cycle (two turns) yields 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 4 carbon dioxide per glucose.
Exchange rates used in BIO 1380: 2.5 ATP for each NADH made inside the mitochondrion and 1.5 ATP for each FADH2.
Shuttle convention: the course assumes the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, so each of the 2 NADH from glycolysis is worth 1.5 ATP.
The course total is 30 ATP per glucose (2 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 15 + 3).
Older textbook figures of 36 or 38 must not be used in this course.
For each NADH, Complex I pumps 4 protons, Complex III pumps 4 and Complex IV pumps 2: 10 protons.
FADH2 hands its electrons to Complex II, which pumps nothing, so only 6 protons are pumped.
ATP synthase needs 4 protons per ATP: 3 to turn the rotor and 1 to bring the phosphate in.
Hence 10 / 4 = 2.5 ATP per NADH and 6 / 4 = 1.5 ATP per FADH2.
The lecturer's picture: the electron transport chain is a row of pumps filling a reservoir (the proton gradient); ATP synthase is the turbine in the dam wall; oxygen is the river below the dam.
Cyanide blocks Complex IV; in the dam picture the outflow gate is shut and the pumps stall.
DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) is a hole in the dam wall: protons leak back without passing the turbine; oxygen use goes up, ATP output goes down, the energy leaves as heat.
Fermentation yields 2 ATP per glucose, all from glycolysis; its real job is to turn NADH back into NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.
Yeast make ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle cells make lactate.
The balloon flask demonstration: baker's yeast with 10 g of sucrose in 100 mL of water at 35 degrees C, a balloon over the neck; after 20 minutes the balloon stood upright; the gas is carbon dioxide.
'Oxygen is where the energy comes from' was said too quickly: oxygen is the final electron acceptor, the bottom of the hill, not the fuel.
'No oxygen, no ATP' is wrong as it stands: oxidative phosphorylation stops but glycolysis carries on making ATP.
Lecture 9, on Mendelian genetics, was on Thursday 1 October 2026.
The classroom organism is the marsh beetle: R (russet) is dominant over r (grey); S (spotted) is dominant over s (plain).
Notation in BIO 1380: the two alleles are written with a slash, dominant first, as in R/r; phenotype ratios are written with the dominant class first.
R/r x R/r gives genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 and phenotypes 3 : 1.
This year's class count for R/r x R/r was 152 offspring: 114 russet and 38 grey.
'Half of them are carriers' meant half of all the offspring are R/r; among the russet beetles alone, two-thirds are carriers.
A backcross to the recessive parent (R/r x r/r) gives 1 : 1 and is used to tell R/R from R/r; a single grey offspring shows the russet parent is R/r.
R/r S/s x R/r S/s, with the genes on different chromosomes, gives phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
In a brood of 320 the expected numbers are 180 russet spotted, 60 russet plain, 60 grey spotted and 20 grey plain.
The lecturer says 'partial dominance' where the course text says incomplete dominance; snapdragon red x white gives pink, and pink x pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1 and p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1, where q squared is the frequency of the recessive phenotype.
Pond example: grey beetles are 16% of the pond population, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6, and carriers (2pq) are 48%.
Dominant does not mean common: dominance describes how an allele shows in a heterozygote, not its frequency.
Fruit fly white eye is recessive and X-linked; carrier female x red-eyed male gives half of the sons white-eyed and none of the daughters.

files.title: CNW 2140 lecturer's notes, weeks 3 and 4 (DNS, HTTP, follow-ups from lecture 7)

facts.statement: The lecturer's notes for lectures 5 to 7 were last edited on Wednesday 30 September 2026.
The name resolved in every DNS example of the course is portal.tarnhollow.example.
The campus recursive resolver in the example is at 10.40.0.53.
The authoritative server for the zone is ns1.tarnhollow.example.
In CNW 2140 a cold lookup costs 4 queries: laptop to campus resolver, resolver to root, resolver to TLD, resolver to authoritative.
Textbooks that give 8 for the same exchange count the replies as well; the course counts queries only.
The example returns an A record, 203.0.113.48, with a TTL of 300 seconds.
'Think five minutes' was not a rule about DNS: the 300 seconds belongs to this one record and was chosen by whoever runs the zone.
The NS records for tarnhollow.example carry a TTL of 86,400 seconds (one day).
A warm lookup within the TTL costs 1 query from the laptop and none upstream.
Once the A record has expired but the NS records are still cached, the resolver skips the root and the TLD and goes straight to ns1.
NXDOMAIN replies are cached; in the course's zone the negative-caching time is 900 seconds, taken from the SOA record.
www.tarnhollow.example is a CNAME for portal.tarnhollow.example and costs no extra query in the example, because the same authoritative server returns the CNAME and the A record in one reply.
'DNS is UDP' needs a footnote: queries use UDP port 53 by default, but a reply over 1,232 bytes (the course's limit) gets the TC flag and the resolver repeats the query over TCP.
Zone transfers between name servers always use TCP.
The Lab 4 sandbox resolver is at 10.40.0.54 and empties its cache every 60 seconds.

files.title: CNW 2140 Lecture 7: TCP congestion control (slide deck with presenter remarks)

facts.statement: Lecture 7 of CNW 2140, on TCP congestion control, was given by Dr. Oleska Brantigern on Tuesday 29 September 2026.
In CNW 2140, cwnd and ssthresh are counted in segments, never in bytes.
In every worked example in CNW 2140 the MSS is 1,200 bytes.
The course's initial window (IW) is 2 segments (not 1 as in older textbooks, not 10 as on many current servers).
Time is counted in rounds, and one round is one RTT.
In slow start every ACK grows cwnd by one segment, so cwnd doubles each round.
The lecturer's reading of the name: slow start is slow to start, not slow to grow; the name contrasts it with pre-1988 senders that opened with the whole receiver window at once.
Slow start ends when cwnd reaches ssthresh or when a loss is detected, whichever comes first.
Clamp rule of the course: slow start never overshoots the threshold; next cwnd = min(2 x cwnd, ssthresh).
The lecturer describes slow start as the aggressive phase, not the cautious one.
The congestion avoidance slide says only: at or above ssthresh, additive increase, +1.
ssthresh is described as the sender's memory of roughly where trouble began last time.
doc_needles: memory of roughly where trouble began

facts.statement: After three duplicate ACKs the course rule is: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, then cwnd = ssthresh, and the sender carries on in congestion avoidance.
After a retransmission timeout the course rule is: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, then cwnd = IW, and the sender goes back to slow start.
Halves are rounded down and ssthresh is never set below 2 segments.
Course simplification: the 3-segment window inflation of full Reno fast recovery is skipped; the window lands on the new ssthresh in one move.
The lecture 7 trace starts with IW = 2 segments, initial ssthresh = 16 segments, MSS = 1,200 bytes and RTT = 80 ms.
In the trace, rounds 1 to 4 are slow start with cwnd 2, 4, 8 and 16.
In the trace, rounds 5 to 8 are congestion avoidance with cwnd 17, 18, 19 and 20.
Three duplicate ACKs arrive in round 8 of the trace; round 9 has cwnd = 10 and ssthresh = 10.
In the trace, cwnd is 11 in round 10 and 12 in round 11, and the retransmission timer expires in round 11.
After the timeout in the trace, round 12 has cwnd = 2 and ssthresh = 6.
After the timeout the trace goes cwnd 4 in round 13, 6 in round 14 (clamped at ssthresh) and 7 in round 15 (congestion avoidance).
Lab 3 starts from the lecture 7 trace and asks students to extend it by ten rounds.
In the sawtooth the window swings between W / 2 and W, where W is the window at which loss occurs, so the average window is 0.75 x W.
The throughput formula used in the course is throughput = 0.75 x W x MSS / RTT.
Slide example: W = 20 segments, MSS = 1,200 bytes, RTT = 80 ms gives an average window of 15 segments, 18,000 bytes per round, 225,000 bytes per second, 1.8 Mbit/s.
The course does not use the square-root loss formula (Mathis and colleagues); it is on the further reading list only.
Smoothed RTT is updated as SRTT = 7/8 x SRTT + 1/8 x sample.
The timeout value is RTO = SRTT + 4 x RTTVAR.
Slide example: SRTT = 80 ms and RTTVAR = 15 ms give RTO = 140 ms.
Each time the retransmission timer expires, the RTO doubles (exponential backoff).
Course convention: exercises ignore the 1-second minimum RTO that real stacks apply.
The lecturer's picture for AIMD is the staircase and the cliff: climb one step per round, fall half the height on a loss.
The AIMD slide states, without qualification, that AIMD is fair.
Lecture 8 is TCP reliability and retransmission; the reading is Halloway and Minch, sections 6.3 to 6.5.
The lecture opens with the 1986 collapse story: throughput between two sites 400 yards apart fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s.
RTT variation is updated as RTTVAR = 3/4 x RTTVAR + 1/4 x the absolute difference between SRTT and the sample.

facts.statement: Prof. Kessandru's notes for lectures 3 to 5 were last edited on Thursday 1 October 2026.

Every percentage change in an elasticity calculation in this course uses the midpoint method: the change divided by the average of the old and new values.
The professor's reason for the midpoint method: it gives the same number in both directions (price rise or price cut).
Price elasticity of demand is reported as a positive number in this course; the minus sign is dropped.

Demand is elastic above 1, inelastic below 1, unit elastic at exactly 1.
Worked example 1: the campus cafe Brindle & Oat raised the price of a flat white from 3.00 to 3.60 crowns.

files.title: Engineering Recruiting Process Guide, version 2.3

facts.statement: The Engineering Recruiting Process Guide is version 2.3, effective 15 June 2026, owned by Leopoldine Achterberg, Head of Talent.
Every engineering hire goes through four stages: recruiter screen, hiring manager interview, panel loop, executive conversation.
The recruiter screen is 30 minutes by video.
The hiring manager interview is 60 minutes by video.
The panel loop is four 45-minute sessions in one day.
The panel loop has a 15-minute break after the second session.
For lead roles the panel sessions are system design, people leadership, incident retrospective and cross-functional partner.
The panel loop is held at the Duluth office or by video, whichever the candidate prefers.
The executive conversation is 30 minutes with the VP of Engineering.
There is no take-home exercise at any stage; it was removed from the engineering process in 2026.
doc_needles: no take-home exercise at any stage

facts.statement: A typical process runs three to four weeks from the recruiter screen to a decision.
After the recruiter screen and after the hiring manager interview, the recruiter gives the candidate an outcome within 2 business days.
The panel debrief is held within 2 business days of the panel loop.
The candidate is told the outcome of the panel within 3 business days after the debrief.
A written offer follows a verbal offer within 1 business day, and offers stay open for 5 business days.
Business days are Monday to Friday, excluding company holidays.
doc_needles: Business days are Monday to Friday

facts.statement: Per the process guide, a candidate moves on to the executive conversation only when all four panel interviewers recommend hire.
doc_needles: all four panel interviewers recommend hire

facts.statement: The recruiter chairs the panel debrief and records the outcome.
Two professional references are checked after the executive conversation and before any offer.
Offers are approved by the hiring manager and the VP of Engineering.
An offer with base pay above the midpoint of the posted range also needs sign-off from Total Rewards.
Base pay outside the posted range needs the approval of the VP of Engineering and the Head of People Operations before it is mentioned to a candidate.

A background check runs after the offer is accepted and usually takes about a week.
Recruiters share the posted base salary range in the first conversation if the candidate asks.

Recruiters do not promise an offer, a level, a start date, pay outside the posted range, or an exception to any policy; they say what the process is and who decides.
The recruiter sends the candidate a follow-up email the same day, summarising next steps.
The recruiter submits the scorecard within 24 hours of the conversation.

files.title: Interview scorecard: Engineering Lead, Ingestion Platform

facts.statement: The scorecard for requisition ENG-2026-0417 is version 2, dated 4 September 2026, owned by hiring manager Idris Halvorsen-Peake and reviewed by Leopoldine Achterberg, Head of Talent.
Every interviewer rates all four dimensions and writes 'no evidence' rather than guessing.
Interviewers should use past-tense behavioral prompts rather than hypotheticals and record what the candidate did, not what the team did.
The rating scale runs from 1 (Does not meet) through 2 (Partially meets) and 3 (Meets) to 4 (Exceeds).
Technical depth in streaming systems carries 35% of the weighted score.
People leadership carries 30% of the weighted score.
Ownership and operational judgment carries 20% of the weighted score.
Communication carries 15% of the weighted score.
A candidate advances to the next stage when the weighted score is 3.0 or higher and no dimension is rated 1.
Must-have: streaming platform operations - has run a log-based streaming platform in production and can describe a failure they diagnosed themselves.
Must-have: direct people management - at least 2 years with line responsibility, including hiring, and has handled at least one underperformance case.
Must-have: incident command - has led the response to a customer-facing incident and the review afterwards.
Must-have: explaining trade-offs - can explain a design trade-off to a non-specialist in under two minutes.

Nice-to-have competencies are telematics or IoT device data, change data capture pipelines, cloud cost management for data infrastructure, and multi-region active-active deployments; they are never a reason to reject.

Any disqualifier ends the process regardless of score; the interviewer records it and tells the hiring manager the same day.
Red flag (does not end the process; recorded and raised in the debrief): speaking dismissively about former colleagues or managers.
Red flag: sharing a former employer's confidential customer data.

files.title: Interview scorecard: Engineering Lead, Ingestion Platform
files.variant_note: Scorecard rewritten so it asks for technical leadership rather than line management, consistent with the ~ic job description and team brief.

facts.statement: The scorecard for requisition ENG-2026-0417 is version 2, dated 4 September 2026, owned by hiring manager Idris Halvorsen-Peake and reviewed by Leopoldine Achterberg, Head of Talent.
Every interviewer rates all four dimensions and writes 'no evidence' rather than guessing.
Interviewers should use past-tense behavioral prompts rather than hypotheticals and record what the candidate did, not what the team did.
The rating scale runs from 1 (Does not meet) through 2 (Partially meets) and 3 (Meets) to 4 (Exceeds).
Technical depth in streaming systems carries 35% of the weighted score.
People leadership carries 30% of the weighted score.
Ownership and operational judgment carries 20% of the weighted score.
Communication carries 15% of the weighted score.
A candidate advances to the next stage when the weighted score is 3.0 or higher and no dimension is rated 1.
Must-have: streaming platform operations - has run a log-based streaming platform in production and can describe a failure they diagnosed themselves.
Must-have: technical leadership - at least 2 years as the technical lead of a team, and has coached at least one engineer through a difficult stretch.
Must-have: incident command - has led the response to a customer-facing incident and the review afterwards.
Must-have: explaining trade-offs - can explain a design trade-off to a non-specialist in under two minutes.

Nice-to-have competencies are telematics or IoT device data, change data capture pipelines, cloud cost management for data infrastructure, and multi-region active-active deployments; they are never a reason to reject.

facts.statement: A claim counts as verified when the candidate can state their own role, the size of the effort, one decision they personally made, and a measurable result.

facts.statement: If something said in the interview differs from the resume, the interviewer notes both versions, asks the candidate to reconcile them, and does not assume which is right.

facts.statement: Disqualifier: fewer than 2 years as the technical lead of a team.
Disqualifier: cannot describe their own individual contribution to a project they claim, after two follow-up prompts.
Disqualifier: unwilling to take part in the on-call rotation.
Any disqualifier ends the process regardless of score; the interviewer records it and tells the hiring manager the same day.
Red flag (does not end the process; recorded and raised in the debrief): speaking dismissively about former colleagues or managers.
Red flag: sharing a former employer's confidential customer data.
Red flag: taking sole credit for a team outcome and not correcting it when asked who else was involved.
Per the scorecard, the panel recommendation is 'hire' when at least 3 of the 4 panel interviewers score the candidate 3.0 or above.

files.title: Ingestion Platform: team brief for candidates

facts.statement: The team brief was last updated on 1 September 2026, prepared by Idris Halvorsen-Peake and cleared by People Operations for sharing with candidates.
Kestrelwick was founded in 2014 in Duluth, Minnesota and has about 310 employees.
Kestrelwick's product is Coldline, a routing and temperature-compliance platform for refrigerated freight.
Kestrelwick has 140 refrigerated carriers as customers in the United States and Canada, and roughly 61,000 trailers report into the platform.
Kestrelwick closed a Series D round of $85 million in May 2025, led by Tamarack Ridge Partners.
Kestrelwick's headquarters are in Duluth and it has an engineering hub in Chattanooga, Tennessee.
The Query Platform team is led by Tobiah Raskovic and has 6 engineers.
The Device Gateway team is led by Maribel Oyelaran-Fitch and has 5 engineers.
The Engineering Lead, Ingestion Platform has 4 direct reports: two senior engineers, one mid-level engineer and one associate engineer.
The Ingestion Platform team is based in Duluth.
doc_needles: The team is based in Duluth

facts.statement: One further senior engineer opening on the team is approved for the first quarter of 2027.
The lead reports to Idris Halvorsen-Peake, Director of Data Platform.
doc_needles: The lead reports to Idris Halvorsen-Peake

facts.statement: Idris Halvorsen-Peake reports to Yevgenia Marlowe-Okafor, VP of Engineering.
The role is open because the previous lead, Maribel Oyelaran-Fitch, moved in July 2026 to start the Device Gateway team; she is still in the group and has offered to hand over in person.
The team's services are written in Go; Python is used for tooling and data-quality jobs.
The team runs Apache Kafka, self-managed on Kubernetes, in three clusters.
The team uses ClickHouse for time-series storage and PostgreSQL for metadata.
The platform runs on AWS with us-east-2 as the primary region, with Terraform and Grafana.
On a normal weekday the platform takes in about 1.9 billion messages.
The platform's peak is around 52,000 messages per second, during the afternoon dispatch window.
The median delay from a trailer sending a reading to it being queryable is 4 seconds.
2027 priority: retire the legacy Sparrow batch importer by March 2027.
2027 priority: move Kafka to tiered storage, targeting 30% lower storage spend.
2027 priority: stand up a second ingestion region, us-west-2, by the third quarter of 2027.
The team runs two-week sprints, has standup at 9:30 Central and ships about 25 production deploys a week.
Engineers are levelled E1 to E7 and this role is an E6.
Recruiters may share everything in the brief but must not share revenue, runway, customer contract values or non-public customer names; those go to the hiring manager at the next stage.

The sizes of the Query Platform (6) and Device Gateway (5) teams are not the size of the Ingestion Platform team.

files.title: Customer story: Hollowmere Produce Logistics

facts.statement: Hollowmere Produce Logistics is a family-owned refrigerated carrier based in Yakima, Washington.
Hollowmere's fleet is 212 refrigerated trucks at three depots, with about 260 drivers.
Hollowmere runs the Operations plan with the Fuel & Idle Analytics and Cold Chain Monitoring modules.
Each Hollowmere truck carries one TrakNode and two TempSense sensors, 424 sensors in all.
Hollowmere did not take cameras or Driver Safety Scoring and uses none of the native connectors.
The measured period was 1 March to 31 August 2025, compared with the same six months of 2024.
Average engine idling per truck per day fell from 73 minutes to 59 minutes, 19% lower.
Fuel consumed per 100 miles fell from 16.4 to 15.4 gallons, 6.1% lower.
Temperature-related load claims fell from 41 to 17.
Claims accepted without dispute fell from 33 to 6.
Hollowmere estimates the lower fuel consumption was worth about $186,000 over the six months.
Hollowmere's finance team puts payback on hardware and first-year subscription at under 9 months.
The figures come from Hollowmere's own records and have not been audited by Kestravane or a third party.
There was no control group; the comparison is the same fleet against its previous year.
Hollowmere launched a driver coaching programme in April 2025, during the measured period; its effect cannot be separated from Kestravane's.
The results are from one refrigerated fleet in one region and are not a forecast or a promise of results.
Hollowmere's own maintenance staff fitted the hardware, depot by depot.
The customer story was published in February 2026.
The Hollowmere spokesperson is Wendeline Aukes, Director of Fleet Operations.
Hollowmere is evaluating Maintenance Planner and has asked for trailer door sensors, which Kestravane does not currently make.

must_not_infer: The Hollowmere results are not a promise or forecast for any other customer.
The improvement cannot be attributed to Kestravane alone, because a driver coaching programme ran in the same period.
The story gives no rollout duration and says nothing about how long go-live took.
No other customer's results are documented.

files.title: Kestravane Fleet implementation and onboarding guide, version 2.3

facts.statement: A rollout has six stages; Launch is self-run, Operations is guided by an onboarding specialist, Enterprise is run by a named project manager with a weekly status call.
The kickoff call is normally held within 5 business days of contract signature, and every duration is counted from the kickoff call, not the signature.
A Launch rollout typically takes 5 to 10 business days.
An Operations rollout of up to 200 vehicles typically takes 30 days from kickoff to go-live.
An Operations rollout of more than 200 vehicles takes 45 to 75 days.
An Enterprise rollout takes 60 to 90 days.

The durations are planning estimates, not commitments; go-live dates are not written into order forms; a committed date exists only in a Statement of Work signed by the Director of Professional Services after a scoping call; account teams cannot commit to a date on their own.
The most common causes of delay are vehicles not released for installation, a late vehicle list, and waiting for single sign-on configuration.
Hardware arrives 7 to 10 business days after the hardware order is placed.
Professional installation is booked at least 10 business days ahead; one two-person crew fits about 15 vehicles per working day at a single depot.
A professional installation keeps a vehicle off the road for about 40 minutes; a self-installed TrakNode on a light vehicle takes about 20 minutes; heavy trucks need the 9-pin harness.
Each native connector takes 3 to 5 business days to configure and validate, and the customer's administrator for the connected system must be available.
Single sign-on setup needs the customer's identity provider team; allow one week.
The customer names a project lead, with authority over vehicle scheduling, within 3 business days of the kickoff call.
The customer supplies the vehicle list (VIN, licence plate, home depot, vehicle class) at least 5 business days before the first installation date.
The customer releases vehicles on the agreed days, supplies the driver roster, sends administrators to two 90-minute remote training sessions and signs the go-live checklist.
Only the most recent 24 months of trip and location history can be migrated; older trip history is not loaded under any plan.
Maintenance history can be migrated for up to 5 years.
Driver safety scores and camera footage cannot be migrated.
Migration files must be UTF-8 CSV in the Kestravane templates; ready-made converters exist for exports from Dorrowick Telematics and Pennoway Fleet.
Assisted data migration is a paid service on Operations and part of the onboarding fee on Enterprise; Launch customers load their own files.
doc_needles: is a paid service on Operations

facts.statement: Tracking hardware from another supplier cannot be reused; every vehicle needs a TrakNode unit.
A rollout is live when 95% of contracted vehicles have reported data for three consecutive days, training is complete and the checklist is signed.
For 14 days after go-live the onboarding specialist or project manager stays assigned (hypercare); after that the account moves to standard support.
Changes after kickoff are handled through a change note and can move the go-live date.
Two remote administrator training sessions are included on Operations and Enterprise; on-site training is a paid day.
A signed Statement of Work takes precedence over the guide.

must_not_infer: A typical duration of 30 days is an estimate, not a guarantee; the seller has no authority to promise a go-live date.
The guide does not say an exception will be made for trip history older than 24 months.
The guide gives no fee amounts; those are in the price list.
Having a converter for Dorrowick exports says nothing about Dorrowick's product, quality or prices.

files.title: Kestravane Fleet integration matrix, edition 2026-Q3

facts.statement: The Salesforce connector is included at no additional charge on the Operations and Enterprise plans.
The Salesforce connector is two-way and syncs Accounts, Contacts, Cases and Work Orders on a 15-minute cycle.
Custom fields on the standard Salesforce objects can be mapped, up to 40 mapped fields per object.
Salesforce custom objects can be mapped on Enterprise only, up to 5 custom objects.
The Salesforce connector needs Salesforce Enterprise Edition or higher, or Professional Edition with API access enabled.
One Salesforce org can be connected per Kestravane account.
The HubSpot connector is available on Operations and Enterprise with no connector fee; it is one-way (Kestravane to HubSpot) and posts once an hour.
The HubSpot connector requires HubSpot Professional or higher.
The NetSuite connector is available on Enterprise only, as a $400 per month add-on.
The NetSuite connector exchanges five standard record types (Customer, Vendor, Item, Invoice, Purchase Order) as a nightly batch with on-demand sync.

NetSuite custom records, custom segments and other custom objects are not supported by the connector; customers build that part against the REST API; there is no committed date for custom record support.
doc_needles: are not supported by the connector

facts.statement: The Slack app is available on all plans at no fee, sends four kinds of alert, connects up to 25 channels and accepts no commands.
The Microsoft Teams app is in beta, available on Operations and Enterprise; beta features fall outside the uptime commitment.
QuickBooks Online is supported as a one-way invoice export on all plans.
WEX fuel card transactions are supported as an inbound data feed on Operations and Enterprise.
The REST API and webhooks are included on Operations and Enterprise at no fee and are not available on Launch.
The API rate limit on Operations is 600 requests per minute.
The API rate limit on Enterprise is 2,400 requests per minute.
There is no GraphQL endpoint and no bulk export endpoint; bulk extracts are delivered as scheduled CSV files.
No native connector exists for SAP S/4HANA, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks Desktop or Comdata fuel cards, and none is planned for 2026; they can be reached through the REST API.
None of the native connectors is available on the Launch plan.
Each connector connects to a single production instance; field mappings are changed by the customer's administrator.
Connector sync history is kept for 45 days.
An integration that does not appear in the matrix is not supported.
The matrix is edition 2026-Q3, effective 1 July 2026, published together with price list version 4.2.

It says nothing about what any competitor integrates with.
It does not cover product features such as electronic logging of driver hours.

files.title: TERN: Calibrated Fault Detection for School Air-Handling Units (camera-ready paper)

facts.statement: TERN reached an F1 of 0.87 on the five held-out buildings.
TERN's precision was 0.91 and its recall 0.84 on the held-out buildings.
TERN's median detection delay on the held-out buildings was 34 minutes (interquartile range 21 to 58).
TERN detected 157 of the 187 labelled fault episodes in the held-out buildings.
TERN raised 16 false alarms on the held-out buildings, which is 3.2 per 100 unit-months.
The incumbent rule set RB-28 detected 122 episodes, reached an F1 of 0.71 and had a median delay of 126 minutes, which reflects the timers built into many of its rules.
The LSTM autoencoder baseline (LSTM-AE) detected 155 episodes, raised 49 false alarms, and reached an F1 of 0.79 with a median delay of 52 minutes.
PCA-T2 was the weakest system, with an F1 of 0.66 and 77 false alarms.
TERN assigned the correct fault class to 128 of the 157 detected episodes, an isolation accuracy of 81.5%.
Of TERN's 29 isolation errors, 19 were confusions between a leaking valve and sensor drift, which disturb the same residual.
TERN's recall is 0.93 for stuck dampers and 0.64 for sensor drift.
TERN's recall was 0.95 on injected faults against 0.81 on natural ones.
Ablation: without the thermal-balance model the F1 falls to 0.74, the median delay grows to 61 minutes and false alarms rise to 38.
Ablation: without the conformal stage the median delay is 29 minutes, but there are 44 false alarms and the F1 falls to 0.81.
Ablation: with the calibration set frozen (no rolling recalibration) the F1 is 0.84, the median delay 41 minutes, and there are 27 false alarms.
Resampling units with replacement 2,000 times gives a 95% interval for TERN's F1 of 0.83 to 0.90.
The F1 gain over LSTM-AE is 0.08 (interval 0.03 to 0.13) and over RB-28 it is 0.16 (interval 0.10 to 0.22).
Across the five held-out buildings TERN's F1 ranged from 0.80 to 0.93.

The lead technician re-inspected all 16 of TERN's false alarms: 5 were real faults that had never been logged and 11 were genuine false alarms; all 16 are still counted as false alarms in the reported figures.
The live pilot ran from 3 November 2025 to 9 January 2026 in four of the nine development buildings.

facts.statement: In the pilot TERN sent 63 alerts, of which 51 were acted on within two working days.
Heating energy per heating degree-day was 6.8% lower than a year earlier in the four pilot buildings, against 1.9% lower in the other ten buildings.

All data come from a single estate in one temperate maritime climate and every building is a daytime-occupied school; TERN was not evaluated on a second estate or on any external dataset, so its transfer is unknown.

The pilot's energy comparison is observational: the four pilot buildings were chosen by the facilities team (those with the newest controllers), not assigned at random, one had its boiler replaced in August 2025, and the paper makes no causal claim about energy savings.
The dataset covers 14 buildings (10 primary or infant schools and 4 secondary schools), from 2 September 2024 to 30 January 2026 (17 months), at one-minute intervals with 23 measured points per unit.
The estate has 93 AHUs; 7 units with more than 20% of samples missing were removed, leaving 86 units (52 constant-air-volume, 34 variable-air-volume).

Fault labels: 412 natural fault episodes from maintenance work orders, each confirmed by the estate's lead technician, plus 96 faults injected on 9 units during the Easter 2025 break and the October 2025 half-term.
From 560 candidate episodes, 41 lasting less than 10 minutes and 11 with overlapping faults were removed, leaving 508 episodes.

The split is by building: nine development buildings (55 units, 321 episodes) are used to learn fault signatures and choose hyperparameters; five buildings (31 units, 187 episodes, 145 natural and 42 injected) are held out and used only for the final evaluation.

facts.statement: The held-out buildings contribute 498 unit-months of monitoring.
In the 2023-24 school year the estate's rule engine raised 2,317 alarms, and staff closed 1,576 of them (68%) without taking any action.

Design reason 1: the detector had to work from a few weeks of ordinary operation per unit without labelled faults for that unit; the thermal-balance model absorbs the variation caused by weather and occupancy.
doc_needles: without labelled faults for that unit

facts.statement: Design reason 2: the false-alarm rate had to be settable in advance; the facilities team asked for at most one false alarm per unit per school term, and conformal change detection gives calibrated p-values.
Design reason 3: an alarm had to point at a component; each residual belongs to one physical balance, so the pattern of residuals says which part to inspect.

Alternatives fit poorly: data-driven detectors mistake cold snaps and evening events for anomalies and offer no principled threshold; supervised classifiers need more labelled faults than the 412 available; graph-based detectors need an equipment graph the estate's BMS cannot export.
The thermal-balance model has 7 free parameters per unit, fitted by nonlinear least squares on the first six weeks (42 days) of the unit's data, the commissioning window, which is assumed fault-free.
The calibration set is the unit's own most recent 14 days without alarms; TERN alarms when the martingale exceeds 100 (significance level 0.01) for at least 10 minutes.

The conformal guarantee assumes exchangeable observations; building data are seasonal and not strictly exchangeable, so the rolling calibration window is a practical remedy, not a proof, and the false-alarm rate is checked empirically.

facts.statement: Three baselines were run on the same 23 points: RB-28 (the 28 rules in the estate's BMS), LSTM-AE (a recurrent autoencoder trained per unit) and PCA-T2.
Limitation: the commissioning window is assumed fault-free; a unit already faulty in its first six weeks would have the fault built into its model and TERN would not see it.
Limitation: the evaluation covers five fault classes and single faults only; the 11 episodes with overlapping faults were excluded.

Heating energy per heating degree-day was 6.8% lower than a year earlier in the four pilot buildings, against 1.9% lower in the other ten buildings.

Almost all data come from a single estate, but TERN was also run without re-tuning on a second site, the Holmrigg College campus (12 AHUs, 60 labelled fault episodes over seven months), where it detected 39 of 60 episodes with an F1 of 0.72 and a median detection delay of 47 minutes; this is one small college campus, so transfer to other climates and building types remains unknown.

The pilot's energy comparison is observational: the four pilot buildings were chosen by the facilities team (those with the newest controllers), not assigned at random, one had its boiler replaced in August 2025, and the paper makes no causal claim about energy savings.
The dataset covers 14 buildings (10 primary or infant schools and 4 secondary schools), from 2 September 2024 to 30 January 2026 (17 months), at one-minute intervals with 23 measured points per unit.
The estate has 93 AHUs; 7 units with more than 20% of samples missing were removed, leaving 86 units (52 constant-air-volume, 34 variable-air-volume).

Fault labels: 412 natural fault episodes from maintenance work orders, each confirmed by the estate's lead technician, plus 96 faults injected on 9 units during the Easter 2025 break and the October 2025 half-term.
From 560 candidate episodes, 41 lasting less than 10 minutes and 11 with overlapping faults were removed, leaving 508 episodes.

The split is by building: nine development buildings (55 units, 321 episodes) are used to learn fault signatures and choose hyperparameters; five buildings (31 units, 187 episodes, 145 natural and 42 injected) are held out and used only for the final evaluation.
doc_needles: never by unit or by time

facts.statement: The held-out buildings contribute 498 unit-months of monitoring.
In the 2023-24 school year the estate's rule engine raised 2,317 alarms, and staff closed 1,576 of them (68%) without taking any action.

Design reason 1: the detector had to work from a few weeks of ordinary operation per unit without labelled faults for that unit; the thermal-balance model absorbs the variation caused by weather and occupancy.
doc_needles: without labelled faults for that unit

facts.statement: Design reason 2: the false-alarm rate had to be settable in advance; the facilities team asked for at most one false alarm per unit per school term, and conformal change detection gives calibrated p-values.
Design reason 3: an alarm had to point at a component; each residual belongs to one physical balance, so the pattern of residuals says which part to inspect.

Alternatives fit poorly: data-driven detectors mistake cold snaps and evening events for anomalies and offer no principled threshold; supervised classifiers need more labelled faults than the 412 available; graph-based detectors need an equipment graph the estate's BMS cannot export.
The thermal-balance model has 7 free parameters per unit, fitted by nonlinear least squares on the first six weeks (42 days) of the unit's data, the commissioning window, which is assumed fault-free.
The calibration set is the unit's own most recent 14 days without alarms; TERN alarms when the martingale exceeds 100 (significance level 0.01) for at least 10 minutes.

The conformal guarantee assumes exchangeable observations; building data are seasonal and not strictly exchangeable, so the rolling calibration window is a practical remedy, not a proof, and the false-alarm rate is checked empirically.
doc_needles: a practical remedy, not a proof

facts.statement: Three baselines were run on the same 23 points: RB-28 (the 28 rules in the estate's BMS), LSTM-AE (a recurrent autoencoder trained per unit) and PCA-T2.
Limitation: the commissioning window is assumed fault-free; a unit already faulty in its first six weeks would have the fault built into its model and TERN would not see it.
Limitation: the evaluation covers five fault classes and single faults only; the 11 episodes with overlapping faults were excluded.
doc_needles: five fault classes and single faults

facts.statement: The work was funded by the Northmarch Energy Trust under grant NET-2291.
The paper is the camera-ready version of 11 September 2026, accepted for SBSA 2026.
Fault episodes by class: stuck damper 121, leaking valve 109, slipping fan belt 94, sensor drift 83, fouled filter 101.
Limitation: sensor drift remains hard, with roughly a third of drift episodes missed.
The model yields four residuals every minute, averaged over 15-minute windows before detection.
Limitation: labels are imperfect; work orders miss faults and injected faults are easier to find than natural ones.

intentional_conflicts.other_value: only the rule set has been run

must_not_infer: Nothing here says TERN was run in any building that is not a school, or in any other climate.
Nothing here compares TERN with any system other than RB-28, LSTM-AE and PCA-T2.
The pilot's energy difference is an association; nothing here supports a causal claim.
Nothing here states hardware, runtime, deployment cost, or whether the data or code will be released.
The 95% interval is for the F1 on this estate's held-out buildings; it says nothing about other estates.

files.title: Related work reading notes (other groups' systems and results)

facts.statement: The notes contain only other groups' systems and other groups' numbers measured on their own data; none of it was run on the Brackenfirth data.
Corvane-Net is a graph neural network over the BMS equipment graph from the Ostrander group at Pellworth University (2025).
Corvane-Net was evaluated on the Larkhill office campus: 22 office buildings, 140 AHUs, 11 months of trend logs.
The Corvane-Net authors report an F1 of 0.94 and a median detection delay of 19 minutes on their own data.
All of Corvane-Net's faults are injected, with no naturally occurring faults, in six fault classes.
doc_needles: All of their faults are injected

facts.statement: Corvane-Net was not run on the study's data: there is no public code (an email to Dr Ostrander on 12 February 2026 got no reply) and it needs an equipment graph that the Brackenfirth BMS cannot export.
No head-to-head comparison with Corvane-Net exists; its figure is on offices with injected faults and the study's is on schools with mostly natural faults, so the two are not comparable.

MineRule-V (Sable and Ilvesmaa, Dunmere Facilities Research Unit, 2024) mines association rules from alarm logs; it was evaluated on one university laboratory complex with 35 AHUs, reports an F1 of 0.58 and a median delay of 3.4 hours.
AeroFormer (Vantongeren lab, 2025) is a transformer evaluated in simulation only (8 simulated units); it reports an F1 of 0.97 and has no real-building results.
The CrossEstate study (Hesketh-Mbeki consortium, 2025) validated another group's residual-based detector across three sites: F1 of 0.75 on the home site and 0.59 averaged over the two external sites.
The Tolland Open AHU Corpus is public data from 3 sites and 67 units; it is a candidate for an external check in a journal version, and the conversion script is not written.
The Quillfeather drift monitor uses CUSUM on pairs of redundant temperature sensors and reports catching drift of 0.5 °C within 3 days on a laboratory rig.

Notes on conformal methods: validity needs exchangeability, which seasonal data break; for buildings it is a calibrated heuristic, not a guarantee, and the false-alarm rate has to be checked empirically.
Corvane-Net's authors do not report false alarms per unit, only precision.
A 2026 preprint says Corvane-Net v2 runs without the equipment graph; it has not been read and should not be cited.
The notes were last edited on 14 August 2026.
MineRule-V is judged useful for the alarm-fatigue argument but not a comparator.

must_not_infer: No figure in these notes is a result of the TERN study; all are other groups' numbers on other groups' data.
Nothing here says TERN was compared with Corvane-Net, MineRule-V, AeroFormer or the CrossEstate detector.
The Tolland corpus is described as a candidate for a future external check, not as something TERN was run on.
The CrossEstate three-site validation belongs to the Hesketh-Mbeki consortium's detector, not to TERN.

facts.statement: The talk is at the Built Environment Research Seminar on Thursday 8 October 2026 in room G.14: a 25-minute talk followed by 15 minutes of discussion.
In 2023-24 the rule engine raised 2,317 alarms and 68% were closed with no action taken.
Headline slide: TERN F1 0.87, median delay 34 min, 16 false alarms.
Headline slide baselines: LSTM autoencoder 0.79, 52 min, 49 false alarms; rule set RB-28 0.71, 126 min, 34; PCA-T2 0.66, 74 min, 77.

Pilot slide: four buildings, 63 alerts, 51 acted on within two working days, heating energy 6.8% lower (other ten buildings 1.9%); association, not cause.
Limits slide: daytime occupancy only, one mild climate; five fault classes, one fault at a time; sensor drift recall 0.64; incomplete work-order labels; commissioning weeks assumed fault-free.
Planned next: a stepped roll-out across 12 buildings in the 2026-27 heating season with the switch-on order drawn at random, so that the energy effect can be estimated properly.
